common_name: Eternal Flame Plant (Torch Calathea, Saffron-Spike Calathea)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in humidity-retentive, well-drained potting mix; unlike most calatheas grown chiefly for foliage, this species is prized for its upright spikes of long-lasting orange-yellow bracts.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light indoors, away from direct sun, which scorches the foliage and fades the bract color. The paddle-shaped leaves are a dark, almost metallic bronze-green above with a purple-red reverse, forming a dense clump beneath the flower spikes. What look like flowers are actually stacked, fringed, orange-to-yellow bracts held well above the foliage on stiff stems, remaining showy for two to three months, a much longer and bolder floral display than other commonly grown calatheas offer. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, maintain humidity above 60 percent with a pebble tray or humidifier, and use distilled or rain water to avoid the leaf-tip browning calatheas show with fluoridated tap water. After the bracts fade, resume a monthly balanced fertilizer through the growing season to encourage the next flowering flush.

common_name: Cascading Calathea (Miniature Calathea, Shimmering Prayer Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in low to bright indirect light in humidity-retentive, well-drained potting mix; its low, spreading habit suits hanging baskets, terrariums, and shaded groundcover pockets rather than upright display.

directions: Grow in low to bright indirect light in a shallow, humidity-retentive pot or hanging basket; unlike the larger, more upright calatheas grown for bold patterning, this species stays compact and spreads by creeping rhizomes into a low mat of slender, glossy, lance-shaped leaves. Foliage is a soft olive to medium green above with a fine, pale midrib and a subtle sheen that catches light, giving rise to the 'shimmering' common name, and a muted purple reverse typical of the prayer-plant family. It tolerates lower light than most calatheas, making it useful in terrariums, bottle gardens, and dish arrangements where taller species would outgrow the space. Keep soil consistently moist without waterlogging, provide humidity above 50 percent, and divide congested clumps in spring to refresh vigor and propagate new pots.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in a well-drained, slightly succulent potting mix; its wiry red stems and narrow, silver-striped leaves form a dense, upright clump rather than trailing.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining, perlite-amended mix; native to shaded forest floors and mossy rocks in Peru, this species carries slender, dark reddish stems and small, plump, olive-to-bronze leaves marked down the center with a distinct metallic-silver stripe, an effect unlike the solid or blotched patterning of most other peperomias in cultivation. The semi-succulent leaves store moisture, so allow the top inch or two of soil to dry between waterings and reduce watering further in winter. Plants form a dense, clumping, mostly upright habit rather than trailing, staying compact enough for a windowsill or terrarium. Slender, cream-colored, mouse-tail flower spikes may appear in late summer above the foliage. Propagate easily from stem or leaf cuttings rooted in a barely moist mix.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in a fast-draining, succulent-style potting mix; its thick, silvery-felted leaves and stems are more heat- and drought-tolerant than most other peperomias.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining, cactus-and-succulent-style mix; native to Brazil, this species carries thick, heart-shaped, gray-green leaves and stems covered in fine, silvery-white hairs that give the whole plant a soft, frosted, felt-like appearance quite unlike the smooth or corrugated leaves of most other peperomias. The dense hairs help the fleshy, moisture-storing leaves resist water loss, so the plant tolerates brighter light and drier air than typical shade-loving foliage houseplants and should be allowed to dry out well between waterings. Its semi-upright to spreading, mounding habit and slow growth rate suit small pots, dish gardens, and mixed succulent-style plantings. Small greenish flower spikes with purple anthers may appear in spring. Propagate from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus briefly before potting.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in a fast-draining, succulent-style potting mix; its tightly stacked, window-leaved stems form slender upright columns rather than the flat or trailing foliage typical of other peperomias.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a very fast-draining, peat-free, mineral-heavy succulent mix; endemic to Peru, this species branches from the base into fleshy, ascending stems densely packed with small, thick, truncated leaves stacked so tightly they form a distinctive segmented column. Each leaf tip carries a translucent 'window' of water-storing tissue that admits light to the interior photosynthetic layer, an adaptation shared with only a few other succulent peperomias and unlike any of the broad-leaved species in general cultivation. Water moderately while actively growing, letting the mix dry substantially between waterings, and cut back sharply in autumn and winter to prevent stem rot. Small, yellow, terminal flower spikes appear in spring. Propagate from stem cuttings, which root readily once callused.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect to low light in well-drained, peat-based potting mix; its deep burgundy-black, deeply corrugated leaves stay far darker than the green-and-silver species and most other caperata cultivars.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a small, well-drained pot of peat-based mix, sized snugly to the rootball to reduce the risk of overwatering; brighter light intensifies the leaf color, while low light produces a more muted, greener cast. Deeply puckered, heart-shaped leaves emerge dark red-purple and mature to an almost black-burgundy, a far richer, more uniform color than the silver-veined green species or the two-tone 'Rosso' cultivar, forming a tidy, compact rosette well suited to small pots and dish gardens. Allow the soil to dry partially between waterings, since this cultivar is as sensitive to soggy roots as the species. Slender, pale, rat-tail flower spikes may rise above the foliage in late summer but are grown as a novelty rather than a display. Divide congested rosettes at repotting time to produce new plants true to the parent's coloring.
